title: Graph Random Features for Scalable Gaussian Processes
claim: Sparse random-walk features give an unbiased low-cost estimate of an expensive exact kernel, enabling scalable inference on structured inputs.
layout: 4 rounded panels, left-to-right then down, arrows between stages, matrices side by side
description: Four rounded boxes joined by thick black arrows show the flow. The left box, "Random Walks", shows a small graph with a blue node v_j and a magenta node v_i. Colored arrowed walks leave each node. An arrow leads to the top-middle box, "Graph Random Features", which shows two sparse feature vectors as rows of cells: φ(i) in magenta shades and φ(j) in blue shades. A second arrow points down to the lower-middle box. It sets the exact kernel formula K_α = Σ α_r W^r next to a dense grayscale matrix, then equals the expectation of the sparse estimate K̂ = ΦΦ^T, drawn as a mostly white matrix. The right box, "Graph GPs", shows the same graph with small orange Gaussian bumps on each node and a few gray nodes. The eye goes first to the colored graph and then follows the arrows rightward.
caption: GRFs for scalable GPs on graphs. The GRF algorithm constructs random feature 𝜑(𝑖) for node 𝑖∈1, …, 𝑁 using random walks. ̂𝐊≔[𝜑(𝑖)⊤𝜑(𝑗)]
abstract: We study the application of graph random features (GRFs) - a recently introduced stochastic estimator of graph node kernels - to scalable Gaussian processes on discrete input spaces. We prove that (under mild assumptions) Bayesian inference with GRFs enjoys $O(N^{3/2})$ time complexity with respect to the number of nodes $N$, compared to $O(N^3)$ for exact kernels. Substantial wall-clock speedups and memory savings unlock Bayesian optimisation on graphs with over $10^6$ nodes on a single computer chip, whilst preserving competitive performance.
